passage:
Friday, 9 June
Result came at 11. I cleared the bank PO exam. Rank 212. Papa cried on the phone, Mummy distributed sweets to the whole lane. Gopika sent fifteen party poppers. 🎉
So why am I sitting here at midnight feeling nothing?
Two years of coaching. Two years of skipping cousins' weddings and the photography club. Papa's dream since I was in Class 8: "a secure bank job, like Sharma uncle's daughter." I said it so often I thought it was mine.
Today I opened my old camera bag, the one I haven't touched since first year. The lens was dusty. I cleaned it for an hour and felt more doing that than I did when the result came.
I don't know what to do with that.
Sangeeta

qa.q: What rank did Sangeeta get in the bank PO exam?
qa.a: Rank 212.

qa.q: Why might Sangeeta feel nothing at midnight after clearing the exam?
qa.a: The goal was Papa's dream, repeated so often it seemed like Sangeeta's own, so reaching it didn't touch what Sangeeta actually values.

qa.q: What turning point does the dusty camera offer Sangeeta?
qa.a: Cleaning the lens stirred more feeling than the result; Sangeeta could make time for photography again and think honestly about next steps before deciding anything big.

qa.q: How might Papa feel if he read this diary entry?
qa.a: Papa, who cried with joy, might be confused and hurt, but could also begin to see that the dream he chose wasn't the one his child held.

grounding: In a diary, a young adult reaches a family-set target and feels empty because it never matched personal values.

passage:
Chinmay: BROOO you made the senior debate team!!! 🎉
Thomas: yeah
Chinmay: yeah?? that's it?? you've been aiming for this since first year
Thomas: everyone in our gang said it was THE thing to get into. so i went for it
Thomas: but i was standing at the selection list thinking… now what
Chinmay: you don't like debating?
Thomas: honestly i like the research part. arguing on stage makes me want to throw up
Thomas: what i actually enjoyed this year was helping at the kids' science camp. nobody clapped for that
Chinmay: dude. that matters too
Thomas: does it? feels like i climbed the wrong hill
Chinmay: then maybe do the camp again this summer. you can still debate if you want
Thomas: yeah. maybe

qa.q: What did Thomas actually enjoy this year?
qa.a: Helping at the kids' science camp.

qa.q: Why does Thomas feel it was the wrong hill?
qa.a: The debate team was the gang's idea of success, not Thomas's own, so getting in brought a 'now what' instead of joy.

qa.q: What choice does Chinmay's suggestion open for the summer?
qa.a: Thomas could go back to the science camp, the thing that felt meaningful, and keep debating only if it's truly wanted.

qa.q: How might Chinmay feel when the big news gets a flat 'yeah'?
qa.a: Chinmay is excited for Thomas and then surprised, but listens instead of pushing, and reminds Thomas the camp matters too.

grounding: In a chat, a student reaches a goal the friend group prized and finds it empty compared with what the student values.

passage: When the letter came from the district office, half the village seemed to arrive in Chandrika's courtyard. She had cleared the constable exam, the first girl from their Punjab village to do it. Her father made everyone sit on charpais for tea. Her uncle made a speech about honour. Chandrika smiled for every photo. Late that night her cousin Amandeep found her by the cowshed, staring at the vegetable beds she had planted: tomatoes, okra, three kinds of chilli. "You're not happy," Amandeep said. Chandrika pulled a weed. "Everyone wanted this so much. I kept running because they were cheering. Now I've arrived, and I only feel tired." She looked at the chillies. "These make me happier than that letter."

qa.q: What had Chandrika planted in the vegetable beds?
qa.a: Tomatoes, okra, and three kinds of chilli.

qa.q: Why does Chandrika only feel tired after clearing the exam?
qa.a: She ran toward a goal the family cheered for rather than one she chose, so arriving brought no real satisfaction.

qa.q: What choice could Chandrika make now, without rushing?
qa.a: She could talk honestly with Amandeep, and later her father, about what she values, like the vegetable beds, before deciding how to shape her future.

qa.q: How might Chandrika's father see the letter compared with Chandrika?
qa.a: For him it means pride and honour for the family; for Chandrika it is the end of someone else's race.

grounding: A young woman in a village achieves the exam goal her family set and feels empty, drawn instead to what she values.

subtype: Linking the goal to the next step [Response]
passage: In the small town of Sikar, Jagdish had one big aim written on the back of his order book: "Own tailoring shop by next Diwali." Under it, his wife Preeti helped him break it down. Monthly: put savings aside, learn blouse cutting, look for a shop space. Weekly: take four extra alteration jobs, one evening of practice with the cutting master, visit two landlords. Every Sunday evening they sat on the roof with tea and went over the list. Some weeks he did everything. The week of his cousin's wedding, he did nothing. Preeti just crossed that week out and wrote, "Wedding. Fine. Next week, two landlords." By August he had the savings and the cutting skill. The shop space came in October, a month late. He opened anyway, a small one, just before Diwali.

qa.q: What did Jagdish write on the back of his order book?
qa.a: "Own tailoring shop by next Diwali."

qa.q: How might Jagdish have felt when Preeti crossed out the wedding week?
qa.a: Probably relieved; instead of feeling he had failed, he could see the plan was still alive and simply move on to next week.

qa.q: Why did the Sunday review on the roof keep the plan going?
qa.a: Going over the list kindly each week let them adjust, like moving the landlord visits, so one missed week didn't sink the whole aim.

qa.q: What would change if Preeti had treated the missed week as a failure?
qa.a: Jagdish might have felt the plan was ruined and given up, instead of opening the shop just before Diwali.

grounding: A young tailor splits a big aim into monthly and weekly steps and reviews them kindly each week with his wife.

subtype: Linking the goal to the next step [Response]
passage: In a café in Valencia, Mateo spread a sheet across the table. At the top: "Pass the nursing licence exam in April." Below it, Fatima had helped him draw boxes: a subject for each month, cardiology in October, pharmacology in November. Each week: three one-hour study evenings and a practice test on Saturday. "And every Sunday," Fatima said, "we check in. Kindly. No shouting at yourself." In November Mateo caught the flu and did nothing for ten days. On Sunday he expected to feel terrible. Instead Fatima said, "Okay, pharmacology moves into December, and we squeeze in one extra session a week. Still possible." Mateo let out a long breath. By March he had only one block left.

qa.q: What did Mateo and Fatima plan for each week?
qa.a: Three one-hour study evenings and a practice test on Saturday.

qa.q: Why did Mateo let out a long breath at the Sunday check-in?
qa.a: He had expected to feel terrible about the lost ten days, and was relieved that the plan could bend instead of break.

qa.q: Which part of the plan helped it survive the flu?
qa.a: The kind weekly check-in let them move pharmacology into December and add a session, so the big aim stayed on track.

qa.q: How might Fatima see the Sunday check-ins in Mateo's plan?
qa.a: Fatima seems to see them as steady, gentle checking, there to help Mateo adjust rather than to judge.

grounding: A young man in Spain breaks a licence exam goal into monthly and weekly steps and adjusts kindly when illness interrupts.

subtype: Linking the goal to the next step [Response]
passage: At the sports club in Kottayam, Anjali taped a chart inside her locker. Big aim: "Certified swimming coach by next June." Monthly: finish one module of the coaching course; assist in forty children's lessons. Weekly: two lessons observed by Joseph, the head coach, and one theory chapter. Every Friday after the evening batch, Joseph sat with her on the pool steps for ten minutes. "What worked? What didn't? What's next week?" When the club closed for three weeks for pool repairs, her chart went blank. Anjali expected Joseph to be disappointed. Instead he said, "No pool, so let's do theory. Two chapters a week till it reopens." She finished the theory early and passed her certification in May.

qa.q: Why did the club close for three weeks?
qa.a: For pool repairs.

qa.q: What did Anjali expect Joseph to feel when her chart went blank?
qa.a: She expected him to be disappointed, which shows she worried the plan had failed.

qa.q: What choice did Joseph make when the pool closed, and why did it help?
qa.a: He shifted the weekly actions to two theory chapters instead of calling the plan off, so Anjali kept moving and finished theory early.

qa.q: How might Joseph feel when Anjali passes in May?
qa.a: Joseph is probably proud, having watched the weekly steps add up, and pleased the plan bent instead of breaking.

grounding: At a sports club, a young woman links a big coaching goal to weekly steps reviewed kindly every Friday.

passage: In the Lisbon library's puzzle corner, Ines always picked the same wooden puzzle, the farm one with twenty-four pieces. She could finish it in four minutes. Bao, from her class, sat down with a new box: a hundred pieces, a lighthouse at night, almost all blue. "Do it with me?" Ines looked at the dark blue pieces and felt her stomach go tight. What if she couldn't find any edges? What if Bao saw her get it wrong? "No, I like this one," she said, and started the farm again. Bao shrugged and began alone. By the time the library closed, Bao had half a lighthouse and a new trick for sorting blues. Ines had done the farm three times.

qa.q: How many pieces did Bao's new puzzle have?
qa.a: A hundred pieces, a lighthouse at night, almost all blue.

qa.q: Why did Ines's stomach go tight at the dark blue pieces?
qa.a: She was afraid of not finding edges and of Bao seeing her get it wrong, so the new puzzle felt risky.

qa.q: What small step could Ines try next time?
qa.a: She could try just the edge pieces of the new puzzle with Bao, a tiny part where being wrong feels less scary.

qa.q: What might Bao have gained that Ines missed out on?
qa.a: Bao learned a new trick for sorting blues by struggling a bit, while Ines stayed safe but learned nothing new.

grounding: A girl in Portugal sticks to a puzzle she already knows because a new one might show her being wrong.

passage: At Friday maths club, Chinmay sir laid out two piles of puzzle cards: green ones the class had done before, and new red ones with trickier patterns. Thomas took three green cards, as always. He solved them quickly and sat with his arms folded. "Try a red one?" Chinmay sir asked. Thomas shook his head. "I might get it wrong." "And then?" "Then everyone would see." He glanced at the others, who were scratching out answers and arguing over the red cards. One boy, Farhan, had got two wrong and was laughing about it. Thomas picked up a fourth green card. He'd done it last month. He did it again.

qa.q: Which cards did Thomas pick at maths club?
qa.a: Three green cards, as always, ones the class had done before.

qa.q: What is Thomas afraid will happen if he tries a red card?
qa.a: He's afraid he'll get it wrong and everyone will see, so sticking with green cards feels safe.

qa.q: What could Chinmay sir try to help Thomas take a risk?
qa.a: He could let Thomas try a red card privately or with a partner and praise the attempt, so being wrong feels normal.

qa.q: How does Farhan's laughing at wrong answers differ from Thomas's view?
qa.a: For Farhan, wrong answers are part of the game; Thomas sees them as something to hide.

grounding: At a school maths club, a boy only redoes puzzles he knows because trying new ones risks being seen wrong.

passage: I'm Devika, Wasim's older sister. Wasim is nine and very good at the number puzzles in the newspaper, the easy ones on Monday. He does them in pen, fast. On Saturdays the paper has a harder puzzle, with a star next to it. Abbu always leaves it for him. Wasim never touches it. Last Saturday Abbu asked him why. He said, "I don't like that one," but he'd gone red, and he left the room. Later I saw him through the door, staring at the Saturday puzzle. He wrote one number, very lightly in pencil, then rubbed it out so hard the paper tore. I don't know what he was thinking. He went back to Monday's puzzle, which he'd already finished.

qa.q: What did Wasim do after writing one number in pencil on the Saturday puzzle?
qa.a: He rubbed it out so hard the paper tore.

qa.q: What might Wasim's going red suggest when he said 'I don't like that one'?
qa.a: It suggests he doesn't truly dislike it but is scared of getting it wrong, so avoiding it feels safer.

qa.q: What could Abbu or Devika do to help Wasim try the Saturday puzzle?
qa.a: They could sit and solve it with him in pencil, making mistakes out loud, so being wrong feels ordinary.

qa.q: How does Devika see Wasim's torn paper?
qa.a: Devika notices how much the hard puzzle matters to him and suspects fear rather than dislike, though she can't know for sure.

grounding: An older sister watches her brother avoid the harder puzzle, sticking to ones he already knows how to solve.

passage: Registration for the state debate round closed at four, and at 3:40 Eshaan was still standing outside the staffroom in the rain, form in hand. Two weeks ago he had lost the district final. He could still hear the judge: "Weak rebuttal from the second speaker." That was him. Since then he had skipped debate practice, told his mother he was "over it", and spent lunch in the library. Mridul ran up, soaked. "Did you give it?" Eshaan looked at the form, the ink starting to blur. "What if I lose again? Then it's not bad luck. Then it means I'm just not good." He folded the form into his pocket. At 4:05 the staffroom door closed. Eshaan felt relieved, then sick.

qa.q: What had the judge said about the second speaker?
qa.a: "Weak rebuttal from the second speaker."

qa.q: Why did Eshaan fold the form into his pocket?
qa.a: He feared that losing again would prove he's 'just not good', so not entering protected how he sees himself.

qa.q: At what moment could Eshaan have chosen differently, and how?
qa.a: At the staffroom door with Mridul, he could have handed in the form and asked a teacher to help with rebuttals, treating the loss as feedback.

qa.q: What might Mridul feel watching the form go into Eshaan's pocket?
qa.a: Mridul, who ran through the rain, may feel disappointed and worried for a friend who seems to be hiding rather than trying.

grounding: With the deadline minutes away, a teenager who lost a debate avoids the next one because losing again would say he is not good.

passage: In the school auditorium in Lucknow, Parul had frozen halfway through her closing speech at the inter-house debate. Twenty seconds of silence, the whole school watching. Her house lost by two points. A week later, the notice for the city debate went up. Parul walked past it three times without stopping. When Harish sir, the debate coach, asked her to sign up, she said she had a family function that day. There was no function. At home she stood in front of the mirror and couldn't make herself say even the opening line. "Everyone saw," she thought. "They all know now that I'm not actually good at this." She deleted the debate club group from her phone that night.

qa.q: How long was Parul silent during her closing speech?
qa.a: Twenty seconds of silence, with the whole school watching.

qa.q: What did Parul believe the freeze showed about her, and why did that make her hide?
qa.a: She believed everyone now knows she isn't actually good, so the freeze felt like a verdict on her worth rather than one bad moment.

qa.q: What could Harish sir do to help Parul face the next debate?
qa.a: He could talk to her privately, say that freezing happens to many speakers, and suggest a small practice with just him before any contest.

qa.q: How might Harish sir read the 'family function' excuse?
qa.a: He may suspect it isn't real and see a capable speaker hiding after one bad moment.

grounding: A teenager who froze in a debate feels her worth has dropped and invents an excuse to avoid the next contest.

passage:
'The inter-school debate list is out,' Dhruv said, looking at his phone. 'Your name isn't on it.'
Yogesh kept his eyes on his cereal. 'I didn't sign up.'
'You love debating.'
'Loved. Past tense.'
'Because of one loss?'
'It wasn't just one loss, bhaiya. It was the finals. I forgot my second point in front of everyone. Mrs Kapoor looked at me like...' He stopped. 'Like I was a joke.'
'You were nervous.'
'No. I just found out I'm not actually good. If I go again and lose again, everybody will know for sure.'
Dhruv put his phone down. 'So you'd rather nobody ever knows, including you?'
Yogesh pushed his bowl away. 'Can we not talk about this?'

qa.q: What did Yogesh forget in the finals?
qa.a: He forgot his second point in front of everyone.

qa.q: What is Yogesh really afraid of if he debates again?
qa.a: He fears a second loss would prove for sure that he isn't good, so the loss feels like it says something about who he is.

qa.q: What could Dhruv suggest as a small next step?
qa.a: He could offer to practise a speech with Yogesh at home, so Yogesh rebuilds confidence before deciding about the next contest.

qa.q: How does Dhruv see the missing name on the list?
qa.a: Dhruv sees a brother who loves debating hiding after one loss, and wants him to notice that avoiding contests also hides the truth from himself.

grounding: At breakfast, a teenager tells his brother he skipped the next debate because another loss would prove he is not good.

passage: At the degree college in Hajipur, elective forms were due on Monday. Kamal had spent every clear night since Class 8 on his roof with a secondhand telescope, sketching Jupiter's moons in a notebook. The astrophysics elective was right there on the list. But Rukmini, who had taken it last year, said half the class got below a B. Kamal's scholarship needed a high average. He ticked "Office Management" instead, the one everyone called a free A. "Smart," said his roommate. Kamal nodded. That night the sky was clear. He carried the telescope up to the roof, then just sat beside it without looking through, and came down early.

qa.q: Which elective did Kamal tick instead of astrophysics?
qa.a: "Office Management", the one everyone called a free A.

qa.q: Why did Kamal sit beside the telescope without looking through it?
qa.a: He may have felt a quiet sadness, having just given up the subject he loves because he feared a lower grade.

qa.q: What could Kamal have done before ticking the safe box?
qa.a: He could have asked the astrophysics teacher or Rukmini about support, or checked what average the scholarship really needs, before letting fear decide.

qa.q: What would change if Rukmini had also mentioned what she enjoyed about the elective?
qa.a: Kamal might have seen the chance to learn what he loves, not only the risk to his marks, and the choice might have gone the other way.

grounding: A small-town student picks an easy elective to protect his average and gives up the subject he loves.

passage: At the university in Chicago, Jamal hovered over the course list for twenty minutes. Music Composition II, the class he had dreamed of since he started writing songs on his cousin's keyboard at twelve. Or Intro to Business Communication, which his friend Bilal said was "basically an A for showing up." Jamal had a 3.9. His pre-law adviser had said, more than once, "Protect that number." He clicked Business Communication. "Good call," Bilal texted. "Your GPA is safe." Jamal sent back a thumbs-up. Then he opened his laptop's music folder, where forty-two half-finished songs sat, and closed it again without playing one.

qa.q: How many half-finished songs were in Jamal's music folder?
qa.a: Forty-two half-finished songs.

qa.q: What does Jamal closing the music folder without playing a song suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he feels a quiet loss; he chose safety for his grades and doesn't want to face what he gave up.

qa.q: What could Jamal try so fear isn't the only one choosing?
qa.a: He could ask the music department whether he can take the class pass/fail or audit it, so he learns without risking the number.

qa.q: Why might Bilal call it 'a good call'?
qa.a: Bilal sees only the grade side and may not know how much the composition class means to Jamal.

grounding: A student in the United States picks an easy course to protect his grade average instead of the music he loves.

passage: In the academic adviser's office at the university in Kochi, Pooja's form lay on the desk. Under "Elective" she had written "Basic Accounting". Irfan, the adviser, tapped the line. "Last semester you told me marine biology was the reason you came here." Pooja kept her eyes on her sandals. "Marine Ecology has field exams on the boat. People say it's really hard. My CGPA is 9.1. If I get a C, I lose the merit list." "Is accounting something you want to learn?" "No. But it's safe." Irfan waited. Pooja thought of the tide pools she had photographed on the field trip, the tiny crabs. She didn't change the form. Walking out, she felt as if she had shut a door very quietly.

qa.q: What did Pooja write under 'Elective'?
qa.a: "Basic Accounting".

qa.q: Why did Pooja keep her eyes on her sandals?
qa.a: She likely felt uneasy and a bit ashamed, knowing she was choosing the safe course over marine biology, the reason she came.

qa.q: What could Pooja still do before the form is final?
qa.a: She could ask Irfan what support exists for Marine Ecology, or whether one lower grade really ends the merit list, and decide with facts rather than fear.

qa.q: How might Irfan feel watching Pooja leave the form unchanged?
qa.a: Irfan may feel concerned, seeing fear of a C quietly outweigh the passion Pooja described last semester.

grounding: In an adviser's office, a student picks a safe elective to protect her grade average and never tries the field she loves.

passage:
Sunday, 3 March
Closed the tiffin service today. Six months, forty-one customers at the peak, and in the end I couldn't cover the gas and delivery costs.
Cried for an hour. Then I did what Charu told me to: wrote it down. Not "I failed." What happened.
1. Priced too low because I was scared nobody would pay.
2. Delivered to four areas; the travel ate everything.
3. Customers loved the dal and hated the Friday menu changes.
4. Never asked anyone for feedback until month five.
Read it to Charu and Mummy on the phone. Charu said, "That's a business plan for the next one." Mummy said, "Your dal really is good."
Next time: one area, fair prices, ask every month.
Feeling sad. But not stupid.
Rekha

qa.q: How many customers did Rekha's tiffin service have at its peak?
qa.a: Forty-one customers at the peak.

qa.q: What does Rekha mean by 'Feeling sad. But not stupid.'?
qa.a: Rekha still feels the loss, but writing down what happened turned the failure into lessons, so it no longer feels like a judgement on Rekha.

qa.q: Which of Rekha's lessons will most change the next attempt?
qa.a: Choosing one area, fair prices and monthly feedback directly fixes the travel costs, underpricing and late feedback that sank the tiffin service.

qa.q: Why might Charu call the list 'a business plan for the next one'?
qa.a: Charu sees the failure as useful information and wants Rekha to treat the list as a starting point, not a verdict.

grounding: In a diary, an adult whose small food business failed writes down the lessons, shares them with trusted people and plans the next attempt.

passage:
Nitin: shut the cycle repair stall today. 8 months.
Hafsa: oh Nitin. I'm sorry 🤍 how are you
Nitin: bad. feels like everyone was right that I'm not a business guy
Hafsa: can I suggest something? write down what actually went wrong. facts, not "I'm useless"
Nitin: ok give me 10 min
Nitin: 1) spot near the flyover, no footfall 2) no spare parts stock, had to send people away 3) didn't track money till month 6 4) repairs were good, people came back
Hafsa: see, number 4 is huge
Nitin: yeah. sending this list to Arvind bhai and my uncle too, they've run shops
Nitin: next time: near the college gate, keep basic parts, notebook for every rupee
Hafsa: that sounds like someone who learned something, not someone who failed 🙂
Nitin: ok. it feels like data now. still hurts

qa.q: Where was Nitin's cycle repair stall?
qa.a: Near the flyover, where there was no footfall.

qa.q: How was Nitin feeling before writing the list?
qa.a: Nitin felt bad, as if the closure proved everyone right about not being 'a business guy'.

qa.q: What choice did Nitin make after writing the list, and why does it help?
qa.a: Nitin sent it to Arvind bhai and an uncle who have run shops, so trusted people can add their view, and planned the next stall around the lessons.

qa.q: How does Hafsa help Nitin see the failure differently?
qa.a: Hafsa asks for facts instead of 'I'm useless' and points out that good repairs brought people back, turning a verdict into data.

grounding: In a chat, a young adult whose stall failed lists the lessons, shares them with experienced people and plans the next one.

passage: Sonali's mushroom shed behind the house in Ambegaon had failed by September. The spawn had gone mouldy in the damp heat, and the few kilos that grew rotted before the Tuesday market. The neighbours whispered. For two days she didn't go out. On the third, she sat on the verandah with a school notebook and wrote down, plainly, what had happened: shed too hot, no fan; spawn bought from an unknown seller; no buyer fixed before harvest. She read it to her husband Saurabh and to Kulkarni madam at the farm advice centre. Madam nodded. "Every farmer here has a notebook like this in their head. Most never write it down." In November Sonali tried again: a cooler corner of the cowshed, spawn from the centre, and a hotel in town that agreed to buy every week.

qa.q: What went wrong with the spawn?
qa.a: It had gone mouldy in the damp heat.

qa.q: Why might Sonali have stayed indoors for two days?
qa.a: The failure and the neighbours' whispers probably made her feel ashamed, as if the shed said something about her.

qa.q: What did writing the notebook make possible for Sonali?
qa.a: It turned the failure into clear causes she could fix, a cooler corner, better spawn and a fixed buyer, which shaped her second attempt.

qa.q: How does Kulkarni madam see Sonali's notebook?
qa.a: Madam sees it as normal and wise, since every farmer has setbacks, and respects that Sonali actually wrote it down.

grounding: A young woman in a village treats her failed mushroom venture as data, shares it with trusted people and tries again.

passage: The class teacher was on leave, and the substitute, Sunaina Ma'am, had a face that gave nothing away. It was the oral science test, five minutes each, and the next class was already crowding at the door. "Nandini, do heavier objects fall faster?" Nandini said, "Yes, Ma'am." Sunaina Ma'am's eyebrows moved a tiny bit. "Oh, no, Ma'am, they fall the same." Ma'am's face didn't change. "I mean... yes, faster?" Nandini's eyes jumped from Ma'am's mouth to her pen to her eyebrows, searching for a sign. "What do you think?" Ma'am asked. Nandini twisted her dupatta. She had read the answer last night. She couldn't remember what she'd thought before she started watching Ma'am's face.

qa.q: What question did Sunaina Ma'am ask Nandini?
qa.a: "Nandini, do heavier objects fall faster?"

qa.q: Why did Nandini keep changing her answer?
qa.a: She was reading Ma'am's face for a sign of approval, and pleasing the teacher mattered more than what she actually thought.

qa.q: What could help Nandini answer from her own thinking next time?
qa.a: She could pause, remember what she read, and say it with her reason, even if the teacher's face shows nothing.

qa.q: What might Sunaina Ma'am notice about Nandini's answers?
qa.a: She may notice Nandini watching her face instead of thinking, which is why she asks 'What do you think?'

grounding: Under time pressure with an unreadable substitute, a girl keeps changing her answer to whatever might please the teacher.

passage: In Class 5 in Pune, Madhuri Ma'am asked everyone to write a paragraph: "Should students wear uniforms?" Vandana started writing no: uniforms were itchy, and she liked choosing colours. Then she noticed Ma'am's neat, pressed saree, and remembered Ma'am saying last week how smart the class looked on Mondays. Vandana rubbed out her first line. She wrote, "Uniforms are very good because they make us neat." As Ma'am walked down the rows, Vandana watched her face carefully. Ma'am smiled at someone else's book. Vandana's heart thumped. She added, "Also uniforms teach discipline." When Ma'am reached her desk and nodded, Vandana let out her breath. At home, she told her mother she still hated the itchy collar.

qa.q: What did Vandana rub out?
qa.a: She rubbed out her first line, which said no to uniforms.

qa.q: Why did Vandana's heart thump when Ma'am smiled at someone else's book?
qa.a: She was anxious for Ma'am's approval and worried her own answer wasn't the pleasing one.

qa.q: What could Madhuri Ma'am do so students write what they really think?
qa.a: She could say clearly that either side is fine if reasons are given, and praise honest reasons, including ones she disagrees with.

qa.q: How might Vandana's mother see the gap between the essay and the itchy collar?
qa.a: Her mother might notice Vandana wrote the opposite of what she feels, and gently ask why.

grounding: A girl changes her essay opinion to what she thinks the teacher likes, anxiously watching the teacher's face.

passage:
'Mumma, is seven times eight fifty-four?' Vijay asked, pencil ready.
Sarita, chopping onions, didn't look up. 'What do you think?'
'Fifty-four.' He watched her face. She kept chopping. 'Or fifty-six?'
'Which one?'
He watched her eyebrows. They didn't move. 'Fifty-four?'
Sarita put the knife down and turned. 'Vijay, you're looking at me, not at the sum.'
'I want it to be right.'
'Right for who?'
He shrugged, cheeks pink. 'For you. You get happy when it's right.'
Sarita pulled up a chair and sat next to him. 'I get happy when you think. Count it out on your fingers and tell me what you get, even if I frown.'

qa.q: What sum was Vijay working on?

qa.q: Why did Vijay watch his mother's eyebrows instead of the sum?
qa.a: He wanted her to be happy, so he searched her face for a sign of the 'right' answer instead of working it out.

qa.q: What is it like for Sarita to realise Vijay answers for her approval?

grounding: At home, a boy changes his answers by watching his mother's face, and she redirects him to his own thinking.

passage:
Dear Madhuri didi,
I need to tell someone, and you're the only one who won't laugh.

Then they asked if the school trip should be to the water park instead of the science museum. I actually really wanted the museum. I said, "Water park, obviously."

Love,
Vandana

qa.a: Vandana said, "Water park, obviously," despite really wanting the museum.

qa.a: He would likely feel hurt and isolated, with no idea that at least one person laughing felt sick about it.

passage: Okay, so the topic this week is "times you weren't yourself." I'm Anjali, Class 12, and mine is basically all of Class 10. My group, Joseph, Nikhil and the others, had strong opinions on everything. If Joseph said a film was rubbish, I said it was rubbish, even though I'd loved it. When Nikhil made jokes about girls who "try too hard" in class, I laughed, and then I'd go home and do my homework in secret, because I was a girl who tried hard. The worst part was that I believed I had no choice. If I disagreed, maybe they'd drop me. It took a whole year, and one friend outside the group, before I tried saying "I actually liked it" about a film. Joseph shrugged and said, "Fair." That was it.

qa.q: What did Joseph say when Anjali finally said 'I actually liked it'?
qa.a: Joseph shrugged and said, "Fair."

qa.q: Why did Anjali laugh at Nikhil's jokes and then do homework in secret?
qa.a: She feared being dropped by the group, so she hid the part of herself that tried hard in class, even though the jokes hurt.

qa.q: What turning point does Anjali describe, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Saying 'I actually liked it' about a film was a small, safe test; Joseph's easy 'Fair' showed disagreeing didn't mean losing friends.

qa.q: How might Joseph have seen Anjali's year of agreeing?
qa.a: Joseph may never have noticed, or may have assumed she truly agreed, which shows how much of the pressure lived in Anjali's fear.

grounding: On a school podcast, a teenager recalls a year of agreeing with friends and laughing at hurtful jokes out of fear of rejection.

passage: I'm Preeti, and I've known Jagdish since Class 3. On his own he's the kindest person, the kind who helps the watchman's son with maths after school. But around the cricket boys he's different. Yesterday at the bus stop, one of them made a joke about the watchman's son's torn shoes. Everyone laughed. Jagdish laughed too, a beat late, and then looked at the ground. When they said the new rule about phones in class was "dumb", Jagdish agreed loudly, even though last week he told me he thought it was fair. I don't know what he really thinks anymore. I don't think he knows either. He just watches their faces before he speaks.

qa.q: What did one of the cricket boys joke about at the bus stop?
qa.a: The watchman's son's torn shoes.

qa.q: What does Jagdish laughing 'a beat late' and looking at the ground suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he didn't find the joke funny and felt uneasy, but laughed so he wouldn't stand out from the group.

qa.q: What could Jagdish try the next time the group mocks someone?
qa.a: He could stay quiet instead of laughing, or say 'Leave it, yaar', and find that one small step doesn't have to cost him the group.

qa.q: How might the watchman's son feel if he knew Jagdish laughed?
qa.a: He might feel hurt and confused, since Jagdish is the one who helps him with maths after school.

grounding: A longtime friend watches a teenage boy laugh at jokes he dislikes and echo the group against his own view.

passage:
Wednesday night
Called home three times today. Once to ask Papa whether to take the morning or evening section of statistics. Once to ask Ma if the blue shirt was okay for the interview. Once just to hear them say "well done" about my quiz marks.
Kishore laughed at me in the mess: "You're twenty, not ten." It stung.
The real thing I didn't say on any call: I want to apply for the six-month exchange in Pune. Theatre and design. Ma cried last year when I only moved to the hostel. Papa says family should stay close.
I filled in the application and didn't submit it. Every time I imagine telling them, I feel like I'm betraying them. I also feel like I'm betraying me.
Ujjwal

qa.q: How many times did Ujjwal call home that day?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: Why does Ujjwal feel like betraying both the family and self?
qa.a: Ujjwal loves the parents and wants their praise, but also wants the exchange, so choosing either way feels like letting someone down.

qa.q: What small step could Ujjwal take toward the exchange without cutting off the family?
qa.a: Ujjwal could first tell Papa and Ma what is exciting about theatre and design, before submitting, so the wish is spoken rather than hidden.

qa.q: How might Ma and Papa see Ujjwal's frequent calls?
qa.a: They may feel close and needed, perhaps without realising Ujjwal is seeking permission for every choice while hiding a bigger wish.

grounding: In a diary, a young adult from a close family seeks parents' approval for everything and feels guilty about a wish of their own.

passage: In Karaikudi, Deepika showed her parents everything first: the kurta she bought, the college elective she picked, the reply she typed to her aunt. She waited for Appa's nod before she felt sure of anything. On Sunday, on the temple tank steps, she told her friend Farida the thing she hadn't shown them. "There's a pottery apprenticeship in Pondicherry. Six months. I've wanted it since the craft fair." "So apply!" Deepika twisted the end of her dupatta. "Amma will say it's too far. Appa will go quiet. And then I'll feel I've hurt them for something selfish." Farida was silent a moment. "Is it selfish to want your own thing?" Deepika watched the water. "I don't know. I love them. I just don't know where they stop and I start."

qa.q: What apprenticeship does Deepika want?
qa.a: A six-month pottery apprenticeship in Pondicherry.

qa.a: She loves her parents and is used to their approval for every choice, so wanting something they may not like brings guilt.

passage: I'm Mahima, and I sit next to Sharmila in the accounts team. For months I watched her say yes to everything. "Sharmila, can you check this report?" "Of course!" "Can you cover my Saturday?" "No problem!" She'd stay till nine, eat lunch at her desk, and apologise for being slow. Last month I noticed she'd stopped laughing at anything, and she snapped at the printer, which isn't like her. One evening I said, "You're allowed to say no, you know." She looked scared. "Then they'll think I'm not a team player." So we made a deal. The next time someone dumped extra work on her, she'd say, "Let me check with Mahima what's already on our plate," and I'd back her up. The first time, it worked. She went home at six.

qa.q: What deal did Mahima and Sharmila make?
qa.a: Sharmila would say, "Let me check with Mahima what's already on our plate," and Mahima would back her up.

qa.q: Why did Sharmila look scared when told she's allowed to say no?
qa.a: She feared that refusing would make people think she's not a team player, so approval felt safer than rest.

qa.q: Why does Mahima's backup help Sharmila practise saying no?
qa.a: It gives Sharmila a gentle, shared way to push back, so she can protect her time without seeming unhelpful.

qa.q: How had Sharmila's constant yes started to affect her, from Mahima's view?
qa.a: Mahima saw her stay till nine, eat at her desk, stop laughing and snap at the printer, signs she was quietly burning out.

grounding: The narrator notices a colleague who never says no burning out, and offers backup so she can practise refusing.

passage:
Note to myself after Friday's team huddle. Reena.
Yusuf has said yes to every request this quarter: two extra client decks, the office party planning, covering Manpreet's calls. Today I saw him eating biscuits for lunch at 4 p.m., rubbing his eyes. When Deven asked him to redo the budget slides tonight, Yusuf said "Sure!" before Deven had even finished.
What I did next: after the huddle I asked him for five minutes. I told him I'd noticed how much he carries, and that the team values his work, not just his availability. We agreed on a line he can use: "I can do it by Thursday, or I can drop something else. Which matters more?" I said I'd back him up in front of anyone. On Monday I'll ask how it went.

passage:
Thursday, 12 October
Maria cried in the washroom today. She thought no one saw. I did.
She's been saying yes to everyone for months. Extra shifts at the clinic front desk, covering for the new receptionist, staying late to file old records nobody even needs. Every time Dr Rao asks, she smiles and says, "Of course!"
After lunch I told her, "You don't have to take every shift. If you want, I'll come with you and we'll tell Dr Rao together that we're both full this week." She looked at me like I'd suggested robbing a bank. "He'll think I'm lazy." "He'll think you're human."
We went at four. Dr Rao just said, "Oh, okay. Thanks for telling me." Maria walked out looking dazed. Then she laughed.
Dilnaz

qa.q: What did Dr Rao say when they told him they were both full?
qa.a: "Oh, okay. Thanks for telling me."

qa.q: Why did Maria look at Dilnaz as if it were a suggestion to rob a bank?
qa.a: Saying no felt dangerous to Maria; she feared Dr Rao would think she was lazy, so refusing seemed almost unthinkable.

qa.q: What choice by Dilnaz made it easier for Maria to say no?
qa.a: Offering to go with her and tell Dr Rao together that both were full made the refusal shared, so Maria didn't have to risk it alone.

qa.q: Why might Maria laugh after walking out?
qa.a: She had braced for disapproval and got none, so the relief of learning she could say no without losing standing came out as laughter 😊.

grounding: In a diary, a clinic worker notices a colleague who never says no and offers to stand with her while she refuses.
